newsitem.title: UK: Dresdner and Deutsche Banks differ sharply on location policy.
newsitem.headline: Dresdner and Deutsche Banks differ sharply on location policy.

text.p: A row over where Dresdner Bank should locate its investment banking business has underlined a sharp policy difference between the German bank and its arch-rival Deutsche Bank.
Dresdner parted with Dresdner Kleinwort Benson chairman Simon Robertson, saying he wanted to concentrate management power in London and that Dresdner felt this to be a "narrow" approach.
Deutsche decided in 1995 that London was going to form the hub of its investment banking business which grew out of its 1989 takeover of Morgan Grenfell, the British merchant bank.

But when Dresdner took over Britain's Kleinwort Benson in 1995, it took a clear decision to split the investment banking between Frankfurt and London in a step which could not be accepted by Robertson.
Both banks are aiming to create a global base for their investment banking business to challenge New York giants such as Merrill Lynch, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley.
But now Dresdner has decided that London is best for its specialities in derivatives and financing but that Frankfurt will dominate for other aspects of the bank's work.
While some bankers say splitting control may cause problems, Deutsche's own experience in Britain has not been entirely problem free.

It has had major embarrassments in its fund management arm in the last year, one of which has proved to be very expensive. DMG faces a large compensation bill and fines after investment manager Peter Young was found to have overvalued investments under his control.
In another high-profile setback, DMG was forced to suspend star fund manager Nicola Horlick in January after the bank accused her of planning to leave the firm and take other DMG staff with her.
DMG has admitted that it was a tough decision when Deutsche decided to put its investment banking eggs very firmly in London's basket, reserving Frankfurt for mark-oriented business only.
Chief executive Michael Dobson has described this as a "bold, aggressive, far-sighted move for which they should be praised."

Instead, Deutsche faced criticism in Germany for apparently turning its back on Finanzplatz Frankfurt and adding to London's already dominant position in the league table of European financial centres.

But investment banks have to be managed from somewhere and while it sounds perfectly reasonable for management to be in the centres where most of the work is undertaken, Dresdner's latest move is likely to be seen as a definite bid to maintain the "Dresdner" in "Dresdner Kleinwort Benson".
Why having managements in Frankfurt as well as London suddenly makes a bank "global" is also a question that Dresdner may face, bankers said.
